title: General Assembly energy package a mixed bag for environmental groups
summary: Environmental groups are in a sticky situation when it comes to the sizeable energy reform package making its way through the General Assembly.
content:
Environmental groups are in a sticky situation when it comes to the sizeable energy reform package making its way through the General Assembly.

Many are encouraged by the bill’s provisions reining in natural gas pipeline replacements, boosting the state’s use of energy storage and limiting multiyear rate hikes.

But language hastening Maryland Public Service Commission approval of power plants is generating concern, as well as what critics see as provisions that grease the skids for new natural gas power plants.

“They put the good things in it [the bill] to make it more difficult for environmental groups or others to decide whether they want to oppose it,” said Susan Miller, a senior attorney for Earthjustice. “Each environmental group has to decide: Where’s their line?”

The bill, backed by legislative leaders, passed a Senate committee unanimously this week and is expected to hit the Senate floor on Monday.

The bill would create a “fast-track” approval process for up to 10 energy projects in Maryland that meet the definition of “dispatchable energy,” which requires them to have a “lower greenhouse gas emission profile” than coal- and oil-fueled generating stations, and to be available to provide energy to the grid a certain amount of the time.

Lawmakers’ touted electric bill refund would average $81 per household

The projects could include natural gas power plants. But the commission must approve four non-emissions-generating projects for every one project that generates globe-warming gases.

The bill also sets a separate procurement process for new nuclear energy projects, and projects that could store energy in batteries to later supply the grid at peak times.

“It’s a very interesting tactic on the sponsor’s part to put a lot of cherries on top of this one to make it look appealing,” said Kim Coble, executive director of the Maryland League of Conservation Voters.

“We remain opposed to the bill that is, we feel, unnecessarily fast-tracking the development of fossil fuel energy sources in Maryland,” Coble said, citing research from the Office of People’s Counsel showing that more in-state power generation wouldn’t be required to meet the state’s energy needs.

Baltimore Gas & Electric, for its part, is “encouraged that the state is seeking in-state generation solutions and taking an ‘all-of-the-above’ approach,” wrote Nick Alexopulos, a spokesman for the Exelon utility.

At least one legislator expressed hesitancy during a Senate committee vote Wednesday about the legislation’s expansive footprint.

“There a lot of different bills added in. Some stuff I like, some I don’t. I’d really like have a little more time than this,” said Sen. Jason C. Gallion (R-Cecil and Harford).

But ultimately, Gallion voted in favor of the bill during Thursday’s meeting of the Senate Education, Energy and Environment Committee.

“A lot of these big bills have little stuff that you don’t like,” said Sen. Brian Feldman (D- Montgomery), the committee chair. “So you just, at the end of the day, you’ve got to weigh it. So none of these bills are perfect, OK?”

Miller said she believes that part of the bill may violate requirements for communities to receive a public meeting at least 60 days before a power generator applies to the commission to build a new plant.

The requirements came as part of a 2019 settlement, resolving complaints that the Mattawoman Energy natural gas plant in Brandywine was built without adequate warning to the majority Black community, in violation of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

The Senate bill, as amended, would shorten the preapplication period to 45 days.

“These things are a product of the settlement agreement,” Miller said. “In our view, you can’t change these regulations.”

Tori Leonard, a spokesperson for the PSC, said in a statement that the commission is “aware of this concern and is looking into it.”

“We will continue to work with the sponsors of this legislation,” Leonard wrote.

The Senate version of the energy bill also directs the commission to “presume” that any site that once hosted a power plant — or still does — is “appropriate” for a new one.

That would allow the commission to essentially bypass a critical environmental justice review, which would assess whether the community is already too overburdened by pollution, said Josh Tulkin, director of the Maryland chapter of the Sierra Club.

“If we can streamline processes? Fine. But Maryland should not fast-track at the expense of already harmed communities,” Tulkin said.

Jorge Aguilar, southern regional director of Food & Water Watch, called the bill’s endorsement of fossil fuel generation “as shameful as it is regressive.”

“The damage this legislation would do to Maryland’s communities — in particular, to low-income and communities of color — would last for generations,” he said in a statement.

In a news release Friday however, some ratepayer advocacy groups and environmental groups chose to applaud other portions of the bill. In particular, the groups highlighted reforms targeting natural gas pipeline repairs and multiyear rate cases.

“These reforms mean gas pipeline spending will cost less, make us safer, and facilitate the transition to clean energy. These reasonable boundaries are a big win for Marylanders,” said Brittany Baker, Maryland director of the Chesapeake Climate Action Network, in a statement.

Emily Scarr, senior adviser at the Maryland Public Interest Research Group, said her organization continues to “question the need and consumer impact of fast-tracking gas and nuclear power.” But PIRG wants to see the consumer protection provisions land on the governor’s desk, Scarr said.

The waste-to-energy industry is also pushing back against a provision in the bill, which would remove trash incinerators from the state’s renewable energy subsidy program.

In a statement, Marylin Lynch, executive director of the Waste to Energy Association, called the policy decision “ill-conceived.”

“The waste-to-energy facilities in Maryland produce enough energy to power 57,000 homes, and it’s mind-boggling that with Marylanders struggling to pay their energy bills because of a lack of in-state generation, lawmakers are willing to threaten companies that provide it,” she wrote.

WIN Waste, which runs South Baltimore’s incinerator, said in a statement that removing the subsidy would push funds out-of-state, and to other waste products that generate energy.

“Let’s be clear – pushing waste-to-energy out of the RPS [Renewable Portfolio Standard] will lead to Maryland dollars flowing to out-of-state facilities creating energy from chicken manure, wood waste, biosolids and landfill gas, not to wind and solar projects as advocates of the bill might have you believe,” wrote WIN Waste spokesperson Mary Urban.
author: Christine Condon
